newsitem.title: USA: Procter & Gamble sues Amway over Satanic claims. [CORRECTED 23:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Procter & Gamble sues Amway over Satanic claims. [CORRECTED 23:55 GMT]

text.p: Consumer products giant Procter & Gamble Co. filed a federal lawsuit Thursday (corrects day) seeking to block Amway Corp. and its millions of distributors from associating P&G and its products with Satan.
In its lawsuit, the Cincinnati, Ohio-based company also alleged Amway was an illegal pyramid scheme set up to enrich founding members at the expense of most of its 2.5 million distributors.
"The principal purpose of Amway is not to sell consumer goods at retail in fair competition with Procter & Gamble," the company said in its lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in Houston.

"Amway's purpose is to divert consumers from the retail marketplace, creating a captive audience which buys Amway products at the exclusion of all others in the false hopes that doing so will lead to riches," Procter & Gamble said in the lawsuit.

Amway said the lawsuit was an "adverse reaction" to an earlier lawsuit dismissed July 14 in Utah, where Amway has filed counterclaims against Procter & Gamble accusing it of publishing false news releases and abusing the legal process.

In a statement, Amway also said it has denounced the "rumor" that Procter & Gamble's "Moon and Stars" trademark is a satanic symbol appearing on P&G products with the number 666, the biblical mark of the devil.
"Amway considers P&G's lawsuits to be a predatory attempt to stifle a growing competitor," the privately held company said in the statement from its Ada, Mich., headquarters.
In addition to Amway Corp., Procter & Gamble's lawsuit was filed against Amway's distributors' association and the Ja-Ri Corp. owned by the DeVos and Van Andel families, which control Amway.

The lawsuit also names several top-level Amway "Diamond distributors" among 16 distributors Procter & Gamble alleged were behind rumours linking P&G and its products with Satan spread through Amway's internal communications and messages sent to low-level members.

Procter & Gamble sought unspecified damages, a court order blocking Amway and its distributors from characterising its products as "evil" and the "devil's work," and ending Amway's alleged pyramid scheme, according to court filings.

According to the lawsuit, 82 percent of Amway products are sold to Amway distributors in a "pyramid scheme" that sends products flowing down the chain of distributors and money flowing back up to those at the top.

The average Amway distributor earned $36.08 a month before expenses in 1996, and half of the distributors drop out every year after they are unable to recruit new members who will pay them commissions on their sales, the lawsuit alleged.
"The promise is basic: If you allow yourself to be victimised today, you will profit by victimising those below you tomorrow," Procter & Gamble said in its lawsuit.
